readerTitle: How many tacos before the food truck breaks even?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (푸드트럭, 1인 배송업체) · 모든 수치는 설명용 · 적용 레슨: 손익분기점(FIN-04-01), 세 가지 이익 레버(FIN-04-02)
insight: 손익분기점은 하루에 몇 건을 팔아야 하는지 알려주는 목표치이고, 세 가지 레버는 그 목표치를 얼마나 낮추는지로 비교할 수 있다.
misconception: 줄이 길면 돈을 버는 것이다. 고정비를 가격으로 나누면 손익분기점이 나온다.

sources.text: 관리회계의 표준 개념 (손익분기점, 고정비·변동비, 가격·원가·판매량 레버)

cards.title: The lunch line is long. The truck still loses money.
body: Maya runs a taco truck. Most weekdays there's a line at noon, and she sells about 35 orders a day.
Yet every month, her bank balance goes down a little. A busy truck and a losing truck can look exactly the same from the sidewalk.

image.label: Food truck with a lunch line and a shrinking money jar
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 손님 줄이 길게 늘어선 타코 푸드트럭, 트럭 옆 유리 저금통에 동전이 조금씩 줄어드는 모습. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표 없이 단순한 타코 아이콘만.

cards.title: How many orders a day to break even?
body: Maya's fixed costs are $4,800 a month: truck loan, commissary kitchen, a part-time helper, insurance and permits. They stay the same however much she sells.
Each order sells for $10. Food, packaging and card fees cost $4 per order. She works 20 days a month.

options.text: About 24 a day: $4,800 ÷ $10 = 480 orders, over 20 days
options.feedback: This treats the whole $10 as money for fixed costs. But $4 of each order is already spent on its own costs, so the target looks far easier than it is.
Each order leaves $6. $4,800 ÷ $6 = 800 orders a month, or 40 a day. That's the **break-even point**: fixed costs divided by what each sale leaves.

options.text: There's no fixed number. It depends on the day
options.feedback: Days do vary. But the average target is knowable, and without it Maya can't tell whether a slow week is a blip or a problem.

cards.title: Follow one order.
body: $4,800 ÷ $6 = 800 orders a month. Over 20 days, that's **40 orders a day** just to cover costs.

breakdown.label: Left over
breakdown.detail: Goes toward the $4,800 of fixed costs

cards.title: Five orders short, every day.
body: Maya sells 35 a day, or 700 a month. She needs 800. Each missing order is $6 that never arrives.
100 orders × $6 = a **$600 loss** every month. The line at noon is real. It just isn't long enough.
Now she knows the number to beat. The next question is which move shrinks the gap.

image.label: Bar of 35 orders falling short of a 40-order line
image.brief: 막대 그래프 한 개. "Sold: 35 a day" 막대가 "Break-even: 40 a day" 점선에 못 미치고, 모자란 구간을 빨간색으로 "−$600 a month" 표시. 깔끔한 플랫 일러스트.

cards.title: Which lever should Maya pull?
body: She can change price, the cost of each order, or how much she sells. Pick the move you'd try first.

options.feedback: The **price lever** is the strongest: each order now leaves $6.97, and break-even drops to about 34 a day. But it's tight. Lose one order a day and she's below again.

options.text: Find ingredients that cost $0.50 less per order
options.feedback: The **cost lever** lifts what each order leaves to $6.50, so break-even falls to about 37 a day. Still above 35, and regulars may notice smaller portions.

options.text: Add Saturday markets: 4 more days a month, with a $400 market fee
options.feedback: The **volume lever** adds 140 orders, but the fee is a new fixed cost. Break-even rises to 867 orders a month, about 36 a day. Still short.

choice.afterReveal: No single lever gets Maya safely past break-even. The next card shows what happens when she combines them.

cards.title: Two small moves beat one big one.
body: Price at $11 plus Saturdays: $5,200 ÷ $6.97 ≈ 746 orders, about **31 a day** over 24 days.
At 35 a day she'd earn about $655 a month. Even if the price rise costs her two orders a day, she still keeps about $320.

groups.label: Orders needed per day to break even (she sells 35)

image.label: Two small moves beat one big one.
image.brief: Labeled HTML chart from the lesson numbers

cards.title: Break-even with nothing for you isn't break-even.
body: Maya's $4,800 doesn't include any pay for herself. Add a modest $3,000 a month, and even the combined plan needs about 49 orders a day.
Averages also hide seasons. A truck that breaks even in June can lose money through a rainy winter, so check the number month by month.
cards.softwareNote: The same math works for a software product. Fixed costs are mostly salaries, and each customer leaves most of their payment, so break-even is a customer count. One new hire raises it the way the market fee did.

cards.title: Now it's a one-van delivery service.
body: Your van lease, insurance and phone cost $3,000 a month. Each delivery pays $15 and costs $5 in fuel and tolls. You do 320 a month, and the van can handle 400.
A client offers 150 deliveries a month at $12 each. What do you do?

options.text: Take all 150 and lease a second van for $2,000 a month
options.feedback: The volume looks great, but the new van has its own **break-even point**: about 286 deliveries at $7 each. With 150, you'd lose about $950 a month.

options.text: Take the 80 that fit in your current van
options.feedback: Each $12 delivery still leaves $7, and no new fixed cost comes with it. That's $560 more a month. Monthly profit rises from $200 to $760.
You protect your **price lever** if other clients might hear about the deal. But you give up $560 a month from spare room in a van you're already paying for.

cards.softwareNote: Watch for the same step in software: a big new client who needs a dedicated support person adds a fixed cost that the deal has to cover on its own.

cards.title: Know your daily number, then move it.
body: This lesson used two ideas from the unit:
list: **Break-even point:** fixed costs ÷ what each sale leaves. It turns a vague worry into a daily target.
**The three profit levers:** price, cost per sale and volume. Compare them by how far each one moves that target, and remember they stack.
cards.callout: **Try it today:** divide your monthly fixed costs by what one sale leaves. Then divide by your working days. Is today's number above or below it?
